title: Identifying and preventing vulnerabilities (part 2)
starter: A company has been hit by ransomware and lost a week of work. List the three changes you would insist on before it reopens.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Passwords
facts: Long passwords, ideally passphrases, with a mix of characters.
Different password for every account, never shared or written down.
Backed up by lockouts and two-factor authentication.
stations.challenge: Describe a situation where a password alone isn't enough.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Long passwords, ideally passphrases, with a mix of characters.
Also credit: Different password for every account, never shared or written down.

questions.q: Which attack do strong passwords protect against most directly?
Give an example of when a password alone isn't enough.
questions.a: When it has been phished or appears in a data breach

stations.name: Encryption
facts: Scrambles data so it can't be understood without the key.
Protects data in transit (HTTPS, WPA2, VPN) and at rest (encrypted drives).
It doesn't stop data being stolen: it makes stolen data useless.
stations.challenge: Give an example of when each type of encryption would be used.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Scrambles data so it can't be understood without the key.
Also credit: Protects data in transit (HTTPS, WPA2, VPN) and at rest (encrypted drives).

questions.a: Intercepted or stolen data being understood

questions.q: A laptop with encrypted storage is stolen. What is the result?
questions.a: The thief has the hardware, but can't read the data without the key

stations.name: Physical security
facts: Locked doors, server cabinets and equipment cages.
Keycards, visitor passes, CCTV and staffed reception desks.
Locking screens, shredding printouts and secure disposal of old drives.
stations.challenge: Survey your classroom: what physical security can you see?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Locked doors, server cabinets and equipment cages.
Also credit: Keycards, visitor passes, CCTV and staffed reception desks.

questions.q: Why does physical security matter for network security?
questions.a: Someone with physical access to a server can bypass many other protections

questions.q: Which is an example of physical security?
questions.a: A locked server room with keycard access

stations.name: Backups and updates
facts: Regular backups mean ransomware doesn't have to be paid.
Keep at least one backup disconnected or off-site.
Patching software closes the weaknesses worms and attackers use.
stations.challenge: Explain why a backup stored on the same computer isn't much use.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Regular backups mean ransomware doesn't have to be paid.
Also credit: Keep at least one backup disconnected or off-site.

questions.q: Why do backups defend against ransomware?
questions.a: The files can be restored instead of paying the ransom

questions.q: Why should a backup be kept disconnected or off-site?
questions.a: Ransomware can encrypt any backup that is connected

stations.name: Match the defence
facts: Each threat has defences that work best against it.
Most real protection comes from combining several.
Your task: place each protection with the threat it stops.
stations.challenge: Complete the matching task on your worksheet.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Each threat has defences that work best against it.
Also credit: Most real protection comes from combining several.

questions.q: Match each threat to the defence that works best against it.
questions.a: Ransomware → Regular off-site backups; Phishing → Staff training and two-factor authentication; Brute-force attack → Account lockouts and strong passwords; Data interception → Encryption, such as HTTPS and a VPN; SQL injection → Input validation and parameterised queries; Malware downloads → Anti-malware software and updates

stations.name: Layers of defence
facts: No single protection stops everything, and any one can fail.
Layering means an attacker has to beat several defences in a row.
Technology, people and physical measures all matter.
stations.challenge: Describe three layers protecting a school's data, from the door to the database.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: No single protection stops everything, and any one can fail.
Also credit: Layering means an attacker has to beat several defences in a row.

questions.q: Why do organisations layer their defences?
questions.a: If one protection fails, others still stand between the attacker and the data

questions.q: Which combination best protects against a stolen password?
questions.a: Two-factor authentication, access levels and monitoring

final.name: Final challenge: build the defences

questions.q: Is each measure a technical, physical or people-based protection?
questions.a: A firewall filtering incoming traffic = Technical; A locked server cabinet = Physical; Staff training on spotting phishing = People; Encrypting laptops' storage = Technical; Keycard access to the IT office = Physical; An acceptable use policy everyone signs = People; Automatic software updates = Technical; CCTV covering the server room door = Physical

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Explain how encryption protects data stored on a stolen laptop.
points: Protects data in transit (HTTPS, WPA2, VPN) and at rest (encrypted drives).
It doesn't stop data being stolen: it makes stolen data useless.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

exam.q: Give two examples of physical security and state what each one prevents.
points: Technology, people and physical measures all matter.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

exam.q: A company has lost data to ransomware. Recommend three measures it should introduce, and justify each one.
points: Regular backups mean ransomware doesn't have to be paid.
Technology, people and physical measures all matter.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 6.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
